claims.text: The baseline NbMoTaW refractory HEA has a homogeneous BCC matrix with minimal secondary phases.
The intervention adds 2–3 at.% Al to NbMoTaW.
The intervention uses controlled oxygen during processing and aging at 1200°C for 1 hour.
Controlled oxygen and aging at 1200°C for 1 hour will promote in situ nucleation of Al2O3 nanoprecipitates in NbMoTaW.
The resulting Al2O3 nanoprecipitates will be fine, coherent, and uniformly dispersed within the BCC matrix.
Fine nanoprecipitates can strengthen an alloy through Orowan dislocation bowing and bypass.
Al2O3 nanoprecipitates in NbMoTaW will impede dislocation motion at 900–1000°C by an Orowan-type bypass mechanism.
Dispersion strengthening by the Al2O3 nanoprecipitates will increase high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance.
The minor Al addition and controlled oxygen content will cause only a minimal density increase.
The minor Al addition and controlled oxygen content will preserve the room-temperature ductility of NbMoTaW.
Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the treated alloy will improve yield strength by approximately 20–30% at 900–1000°C.
Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the treated alloy will improve creep resistance by approximately 20–30% at 900–1000°C.
The treated alloy will show no significant degradation in room-temperature tensile ductility.
Formation of non-coherent or insufficient oxide precipitates would negate the proposed high-temperature strengthening.
Improper oxygen control or aging parameters could reduce high-temperature performance.
The hypothesis is intended to hold under creep and tensile loading at 900–1000°C.
TEM can be used to assess precipitate presence, size distribution, and coherency after processing.
Failure to form suitable Al2O3 precipitates or failure to achieve at least a 20% high-temperature mechanical improvement would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the intervention maintains low density, while the mechanism explicitly anticipates a density increase, albeit a minimal one.
